column4: ### Genesis: The God Who Dwells With His Creation
column5: ### Genesis: The God Who Dwells with His Creation

column4: A central theme in the narrative of God is His **desire to dwell** with His creation. This is clear in the stories throughout Genesis. Across its fifty chapters and genealogies from Adam (the first man) through Joseph (that last major figure in the book of Genesis, the last significant leader of God’s people before Moses), there is a period of approximately ~2,400 years. We can see through these stories the consistency of God’s goodness despite man’s wickedness.
column5: A central theme in God’s story is his desire to dwell with his creation. This is clearly seen in the narratives in Genesis. Within its fifty chapters and genealogies beginning with Adam (the first man) to Joseph (who is the last major figure in the book of Genesis, the last significant leader of God’s people before Moses), there is a span of approximately ~2,400 years. In these stories we see the constancy of God’s goodness despite human evil.

column4: 1.  **Adam and Eve** - The first humans, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden. God walks and talks with them, giving them instructions and establishing a relationship of mutual love and obedience. However, this relationship is impacted by their disobedience in eating from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil (Genesis 1-3).
column5: 1.  **Adam and Eve** - The first humans, created by God, and placed in the Garden of Eden. God walked with them and spoke to them, giving instructions and building a mutual relationship of love and obedience. However, that relationship was affected by their disobedience when they ate from the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil (Genesis 1-3).

column4: 2.  **Cain** - Although Cain ultimately rebels by murdering his brother Abel, God speaks directly to him, warning him about the danger of sin and offering him guidance before the murder. Even after Cain’s punishment, God marks him to protect him from harm (Genesis 4).
column5: 2.  **Cain** - Although Cain ultimately committed the murder of his brother Abel, God spoke to him directly, warning him of the danger of sin and giving him guidance before the killing. Even after Cain’s punishment, God set a mark for him to protect him from harm (Genesis 4).

column4: 3.  **Noah** - God establishes a unique relationship with Noah, a righteous man, in a time of widespread corruption. God commands Noah to build an ark to save his family and the animals from the Flood. Afterward, God makes a covenant with Noah, promising never again to destroy the earth with a flood and establishing the rainbow as a sign of this covenant (Genesis 6-9).
column5: 3.  **Noah** - God formed a special relationship with Noah, a righteous man, at a time when corruption was very widespread. God commanded Noah to build an ark to save his family and the animals from the coming flood. Afterwards, God made a covenant with Noah, promising not to destroy the earth again with a flood, and set the rainbow as the sign of that covenant (Genesis 6-9).

column4: 4.  **Abraham (Abram)** - One of the most significant relationships in Genesis, God calls Abram to leave his homeland and promises to make him the father of a great nation. God establishes a covenant with Abram, promising land, descendants, and blessings for all nations through him. Abram’s faith and obedience become central themes, and his name is changed to Abraham as part of the covenant (Genesis 12, 15, 17, 22).
column5: 4.  **Abraham (Abram)** - One of the most important relationships in Genesis, God called Abram to leave his homeland and promised to make him the father of a great nation. column4: 5.  **Hagar** - An Egyptian servant of Sarah, Hagar encounters God in the wilderness after being mistreated. God comforts her, promises her a future for her son Ishmael, and instructs her to return to Abraham and Sarah. Hagar refers to God as “El Roi” (“The God Who Sees Me”), recognizing His care for her (Genesis 16).

column4: 6.  **Isaac** - The son of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac inherits the covenant promises made to his father. column5: 6.  **Isaac** - The son of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac inherits his father’s covenant promises. God confirms these promises directly to Isaac, including the promise of offspring and blessings. column4: 7.  **Rebekah** - Although her relationship with God is indirect, God answers Rebekah’s prayer about her difficult pregnancy, revealing that her twins, Jacob and Esau, will become two nations with distinct destinies (Genesis 25).
column5: 7.  **Rebekah** - Although her relationship with God was indirect, God answered Rebekah’s prayer regarding her difficult pregnancy, revealing that her twins, Jacob and Esau, would become two nations with different destinies (Genesis 25).

column4: 8.  **Jacob** - God establishes a personal relationship with Jacob, appearing to him in a dream and confirming the covenant promises of land, descendants, and blessings. column4: 9.  **Joseph** - Although Joseph’s relationship with God isn’t based on direct appearances or covenants like those of Abraham or Jacob, God is deeply involved in his life. Joseph’s faith in God’s sovereignty allows him to forgive his brothers, recognizing that God used his suffering for good (Genesis 37, 39-50).

column5: Throughout this whole story God, desiring to dwell with His creation, was compelled to dwell with a particular chosen group, and ultimately, by making a covenant with Abraham, He established a nation (Genesis 17:7).

column4: God’s desire to dwell with His people is also clearly seen in the second book of the Bible, Exodus. In the book of the exodus the people of Israel, who had lived for a period of time in relative peace and harmony in Egypt, are now being oppressed by a Pharaoh who did not know of Joseph and feared the Hebrews (Exodus 1:6-8). God’s people lived in Egypt for roughly ~400 years (Exodus 12:40-41), of which the later portion of that was spent living as slaves (there is not a universal consensus on precisely how long Israel was in bondage to Egypt).

column4: The phrase **“I AM THAT I AM”** (Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh) is one of the most profound self-revelations in Scripture. When Moses asks for God’s name, God responds with this phrase, which can be translated as "I Am Who I Am," "I Will Be Who I Will Be," or simply "I Am." This declaration on the surface is a bit confusing but holds deep meaning. Could you imagine introducing yourself to someone new as ‘I am’? When God reveals Himself as ‘I AM THAT I AM’ He is attesting to His nature, His eternal presence, His sovereignty. ‘I am’ is infinite in meaning and purpose.

column4: ### The Rest of the Old Testament
column5: ### The Rest of the Old Testament

column4: In the ~1,400 years between the death of Moses and the birth of Christ the Israelites experienced a recurring cycle of devotion which brings God's favor and blessings, followed by rebellion, God’s judgment, their subsequent repentance, and ultimately God’s deliverance. This pattern is particularly evident in the books of **Judges, Kings, and Chronicles**, which recount cycles where the people turn away from God, often by worshiping other gods, resulting in periods of oppression or exile. In response to their cries, God repeatedly raised up judges, prophets, or leaders to deliver them.
column5: For nearly 1,400 years between the death of Moses and the birth of the Messiah, the Israelites experienced a recurring cycle: faithfulness leading to God’s favor and blessings, then disobedience, God’s judgment, their repentance, and finally God’s deliverance. This pattern is especially seen in the books of **Judges, Kings, and Chronicles**, which recount cycles of the people turning away from God, often worshiping other gods, resulting in periods of oppression or exile. When they cry out, God repeatedly raises up judges, prophets, or leaders to deliver them.

column4: Throughout these years, despite the Israelites' frequent failures to uphold their covenant with Him, God remains faithful, showing both justice and mercy. He continuously rescues and forgives His people, demonstrating His enduring commitment and love.
column5: Throughout these years, although the Israelites often failed to keep their covenant with Him, God remained faithful, demonstrating both justice and mercy. He continually delivers and forgives His people, revealing His commitment and enduring love.

column4: God’s character and actions are fully expressed in the unity of Father, Son, and Spirit. The scriptures teach that God is one in essence, yet exists as three distinct persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Scripture affirms God’s oneness, stating, “beside Him there is no God” (Isaiah 45:5). However, the Godhead is understood as a **compound unity**-three distinct persons who cooperate with a singular mind and purpose, united in the truest sense. Each person of the Trinity has a unique role: the **Father creates**, the **Son redeems**, and the **Holy Spirit sanctifies**. The term “Trinity” does not appear in the Bible; it was developed as a theological expression to describe this concept, which is revealed through Scripture.
column5: The character and actions of God are fully revealed in the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. Scripture teaches that God is essentially one, yet there are three distinct Persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Scripture affirms God’s oneness, saying, “There is no other God besides Me” (Isaiah 45:5). Nevertheless, the Godhead is understood as a composite unity—three distinct Persons cooperating in one mind and purpose, united in the truest sense. Each Person of the Trinity has a particular role: **the Father creates**, **the Son redeems**, **the Holy Spirit sanctifies**. The word “Trinity” does not appear in the Bible; it became a theological expression used to describe this concept, which Scripture illuminates.

column4: The Trinity can be illustrated by examples in nature, which help clarify this idea of unity in diversity. Like water, which can be liquid, ice, or vapor but remains H₂O, each person of the Trinity is fully God yet distinct in personhood. Or consider a triangle, with three sides and three angles, forming one complete shape; if one side is removed, it ceases to be a triangle. Similarly, **God’s nature is incomplete without all three persons**, who work together in perfect unity.
column5: The Trinity can be illustrated by natural analogies that help clarify the idea of unity in diversity. Like water, which can be liquid, ice, or vapor, yet is still H₂O, each Person of the Trinity is fully God while personally distinct. Or consider a triangle, with three sides and three angles, forming one complete shape; if one side is removed, it is no longer a triangle. Likewise, **God’s nature is not complete without these three Persons**, who work together perfectly in unity.

column4: - **God the Father**: He is the creator and sustainer of all things, often understood as the initiator in the Godhead. His love for humanity is central to the biblical story, exemplified in John 3:16. In our study we will examine God the father as the loving father and righteous judge, who made a path for our redemption.
column5: - **God the Father**: He is the Creator and sustainer of all things, often understood as the source within the Godhead. His love for humanity is central to the biblical story, as shown in John 3:16. In our study we will consider God the Father as a loving Father and a righteous Judge, who made the way for our redemption.

column4: - **God the Son**: Co-existent and co-eternal with the Father, Jesus took on human nature, being conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. He lived a sinless life, died to redeem humanity, and rose again, defeating sin and death. He now sits at the Father’s right hand, interceding for us (John 1:1-3; Matthew 1:23; 1 Timothy 2:5). In our study we will examine Jesus as the perfect atoning sacrifice, the resurrected Lord, and head of the church.
column5: - **The Son of God**: Of the same essence and eternally equal with the Father, Jesus took on human nature, being conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. He lived a sinless life, died to redeem humanity, and rose again, conquering sin and death. He now sits at the Father’s right hand, interceding for us (John 1:1-3; Matthew 1:23; 1 Timothy 2:5). In our study we will consider Jesus as the perfect sacrifice for sin, the risen Lord, and the head of the church.

column4: - **God the Holy Spirit**: The Holy Spirit, co-existent and equal with the Father and the Son, is sent by the Father through the Son to convict the world of sin and prepare believers as the Bride of Christ. He empowers, comforts, and sanctifies those who are in Christ (John 14:26; 15:26; 16:8). In our study we will examine the Holy Spirit as the comforter, given to us by God to equip, empower, sanctify, and abide with us.
column5: - **God the Holy Spirit**: The Holy Spirit, co-existent and equal with the Father and the Son, was sent by the Father through the Son to convict the world of sin and to prepare believers as the Bride of Christ. He empowers, comforts, and sanctifies those who are in Christ (John 14:26; 15:26; 16:8). In our study we will consider the Holy Spirit as Counselor and Helper, whom God has given to equip us, strengthen us, sanctify us, and be with us.

column4: Through these distinct persons, God’s triune nature is revealed as a perfect union in purpose, will, and love, each person playing a vital role in the divine mission of creation, redemption, and sanctification. The Trinity invites believers to experience God fully, both as a loving Father, a redeeming Savior, and a transforming Spirit.
column5: Through these distinct Persons, the triune nature of God is revealed in perfect unity of purpose, will, and love, and each Person plays an indispensable role in the divine mission of creation, redemption, and sanctification. The Trinity invites believers to experience God fully—as a loving Father, a redeeming Savior, and a transforming Spirit.

column4: ## Conclusion
column5: ## Conclusion

column4: We can be uniquely known by our names: husband, father, son, brother, friend. Each of these a declaration of who we are in relation to someone else. We can also be known by our attributes: faithful, patient, kind, intelligent, funny. Likewise, we can know God by His attributes and names- He is our Healer, Provider, Shepherd, and Redeemer. However, as labels and words are only a small part of us, for ourselves to be truly known by others, we must be experienced. Even more so with God. To truly and fully know Him we must experience Him.
column5: Our names can set us apart: spouse, father, son, brother, friend. Each is a statement of what we are in relation to someone else. We can also be known by attributes: faithful, patient, compassionate, intelligent, humorous. Likewise, we can know God by His attributes and His names—He is our Healer, our Provider, our Shepherd, and our Redeemer. Yet, just as labels and words capture only a small part of us, to be truly known we must be experienced. Even more so with God. To know Him truly and fully, He must be experienced.

column4: God’s names reveal His character, but personal encounters deepen our understanding of what these names signify. For instance, “God my Healer” takes on a richer, more profound meaning when we understand the depths of illness, desperation, or helplessness from which God rescues. Knowing Him as our Provider is transformed when we have felt true need and found Him faithful.
column5: The names of God reveal His character, but personal encounters deepen our understanding of what these names mean. For example, “my God the Healer” takes on deeper meaning when we grasp the depths of illness, despair, or weakness from which God has delivered us. Knowing Him as Provider is transformed when we have felt real need and have found Him faithful.

column4: Scriptures offer a context to these encounters, showing us God’s faithfulness to His people across time and circumstance, reinforcing how His names and attributes are not mere titles but realities He brings to life, experienced in the lives of individuals. It is through this interplay of personal experience and the scriptural narrative that we come to know God-not just as a distant description but as a present, active relationship in every season of our lives.

It is through the interplay of personal experience and the scriptural story that we come to know God—not as a distant description, but as a continual, dynamic relationship in every season of our lives.
